header:
How index funds
took over Wall Street

lines.text: In 1976, Wall Street laughed at this fund.
lines.say: In nineteen seventy-six, Wall Street laughed at this fund.

lines.text: Fifty years later, it holds more than $1.6 trillion.
lines.say: Fifty years later, that same fund holds more than one point six trillion dollars.

lines.text: And the boring idea behind it took over Wall Street.
lines.say: And the idea behind it, which is honestly kind of boring, went on to take over Wall Street.

lines.text: By the end of 2025, passive funds held over 55% of US fund assets.
lines.say: By the end of twenty twenty-five, index-tracking funds held more than fifty-five percent of all US fund assets.

lines.text: Warren Buffett even bet on it against hedge funds.
lines.say: Warren Buffett even bet on it against a group of hedge funds. We'll get to who won.

lines.text: So how did a fund nobody wanted end up owning a slice of almost everything?
lines.say: So how did a fund nobody wanted end up owning a slice of almost everything?

lines.text: The plan: how it started, why fees matter, who wins, and is it too big?
lines.say: Here's the plan: how it started, why fees matter, who actually wins, and whether index funds got too big.

lines.text: Education, not advice. Just how it works.
lines.say: Quick note: this is education, not advice. No fund picks and no predictions, just how the machine works.

lines.text: Chapter 1: The boring idea
lines.say: Chapter one: the boring idea.

lines.text: An index is a scoreboard for a group of stocks.
lines.say: First, an index is just a scoreboard for a group of stocks. The S and P five hundred tracks about five hundred big US companies.

lines.text: An index fund buys every stock on the scoreboard.
lines.say: An index fund simply buys every stock on that scoreboard, in the same proportions, so it matches the score instead of trying to beat it.

lines.text: Example: $100 in an S&P 500 index fund buys a sliver of all 500 companies.
lines.say: For example, put a hundred dollars into an S and P five hundred index fund, and you own a tiny sliver of all five hundred companies.

lines.text: Active funds pick stocks. Index funds copy the index.
lines.say: That's the big split. An active fund pays a manager to pick winners and beat the market. An index fund, called passive, skips the picking and copies the index.

scene.title: Two ways to run a fund

lines.text: No star manager. No hot tips.
lines.say: No star manager, no hot tips, no genius. Which is exactly why Wall Street hated it at first.

lines.text: 1971: Wells Fargo builds an early index fund.
lines.say: The first real attempt came in nineteen seventy-one, at Wells Fargo.

lines.text: A $6 million portfolio for Samsonite's pension, holding every NYSE stock.
lines.say: It built a six million dollar portfolio for Samsonite's pension plan, holding every stock on the New York Stock Exchange.

lines.text: Equal weights meant constant rebalancing.
lines.say: But it gave every stock an equal weight, which meant constant trading to rebalance.

lines.text: Costs piled up, so it switched to the S&P 500.
lines.say: The costs piled up, so a few years later it switched to tracking the S and P five hundred.

lines.text: It was for big pensions only.
lines.say: And that fund was built for a big pension plan. Regular savers couldn't buy in.

lines.text: Aug 31, 1976: Vanguard opens the first index mutual fund.
lines.say: That changed on August thirty-first, nineteen seventy-six, when Jack Bogle's Vanguard opened the First Index Investment Trust, a fund anyone could buy.

lines.text: The goal: $150 million. It raised $11.3 million.
lines.say: The goal was to raise one hundred fifty million dollars. It raised eleven point three million.

lines.text: It could afford only 280 of the 500 stocks at first.
lines.say: That was so little money that the fund could only afford two hundred eighty of the five hundred stocks at first.

lines.text: They called it 'Bogle's Folly' and 'un-American.'
lines.say: The industry nicknamed it Bogle's Folly, and some called indexing un-American. Bogle himself called the launch a complete flop.

lines.text: Who pays to be average?
lines.say: The knock on it was simple: who would pay to be merely average?

lines.text: Jan 1993: SPY, the first US ETF, launches.
lines.say: Then, in January nineteen ninety-three, the spider S and P five hundred E T F, ticker S P Y, launched as the first US exchange-traded fund.

lines.text: An ETF is an index fund that trades all day like a stock.
lines.say: An E T F is a fund, often an index fund, that trades on an exchange all day, like a stock.

lines.text: SPY held more than $800 billion in late September 2026.
lines.say: As of late September twenty twenty-six, S P Y alone held more than eight hundred billion dollars.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Why cheap wins
lines.say: Chapter two: why cheap wins.

lines.text: Expense ratio = a % of your balance, every year.
lines.say: Every fund charges an expense ratio: a percentage of your balance, taken quietly out of your returns every year.

lines.text: 2025 average: index stock funds 0.05%, active 0.64% (ICI).
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, the average index stock mutual fund charged zero point zero five percent. The average active one charged zero point six four percent, says the Investment Company Institute.

lines.text: That's nearly 13 times more for active.
lines.say: That's nearly thirteen times more for the active fund.

lines.text: On $10,000: $5 a year versus $64 a year.
lines.say: On ten thousand dollars, that's five dollars a year versus sixty-four dollars a year.

lines.text: Index stock fund fees: 0.27% in 1996, 0.09% by 2016.
lines.say: And index fees kept falling: zero point two seven percent in nineteen ninety-six, and zero point zero nine percent by twenty sixteen.

lines.text: 0.05% by 2022, still 0.05% in 2025: down more than 80% since 1996.
lines.say: By twenty twenty-two it hit zero point zero five percent, and it stayed there in twenty twenty-five, down more than eighty percent since nineteen ninety-six.

lines.text: Active stock funds fell too: 1.08% (1996) to 0.64% (2025).
lines.say: Active stock funds got cheaper too, from one point zero eight percent in nineteen ninety-six to zero point six four percent in twenty twenty-five. The gap never closed.

lines.text: Does a fraction of a percent really matter?
lines.say: So does a fraction of a percent really matter? Let's do the math.

lines.text: Example: $10,000, 30 years, 7% a year before fees (an assumption).
lines.say: Here's a made-up example: ten thousand dollars, left alone for thirty years, earning an assumed seven percent a year before fees. That's not a prediction.

lines.text: Value = $10,000 x (1 + 7% - fee) to the 30th power.
lines.say: The fee comes off the return each year, so the math is ten thousand dollars times one plus seven percent minus the fee, to the thirtieth power.

lines.text: At 0.05%: grows 6.95% a year, ends at $75,063.
lines.say: At the index fee, the money grows six point nine five percent a year and ends at about seventy-five thousand and sixty-three dollars.

lines.text: At 0.64%: grows 6.36% a year, ends at $63,584.
lines.say: At the active fee, it grows six point three six percent a year and ends at about sixty-three thousand five hundred eighty-four dollars.

lines.text: Same money, same market, same 30 years.
lines.say: Same money, same market, same thirty years.

lines.text: The gap: $11,478, about 15% of the low-fee result.
lines.say: The gap is about eleven thousand four hundred seventy-eight dollars, roughly fifteen percent of the low-fee result, lost to fees alone.

lines.text: Versus no fee: 0.64% costs $12,538; 0.05% costs $1,060.
lines.say: Compared with no fee at all, the zero point six four percent fee costs about twelve thousand five hundred thirty-eight dollars. The low fee costs about one thousand and sixty.

lines.text: Fees compound, just like returns.
lines.say: Fees compound just like returns, because every dollar paid in fees stops growing too.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Who actually wins?
lines.say: Chapter three: who actually wins?

lines.text: But can a great stock picker earn that fee back?
lines.say: Okay, cheap is nice. But what if a good manager earns that fee back by picking better stocks?

lines.text: S&P's SPIVA scorecard checks active funds against their index, after fees.
lines.say: S and P Dow Jones Indices tracks this in its SPIVA scorecard, comparing active funds with their index after fees.

lines.text: In 2025, 79% of active large-cap funds trailed the S&P 500.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, seventy-nine percent of active large-cap US stock funds trailed the S and P five hundred.

lines.text: Over 10 years: more than 8 in 10 trailed. Over 15 years: about 9 in 10.
lines.say: One year can be luck. But over the ten years to the end of twenty twenty-five, more than eight in ten trailed. Over fifteen years, about nine in ten.

lines.text: Funds that closed or merged count as losers.
lines.say: And funds that closed or merged count as losers, so bad ones can't quietly vanish from the record.

lines.text: Buffett's famous bet.
lines.say: Then came the most famous test, from Warren Buffett.

scene.headline: Buffett bets on an index fund

lines.text: He bet an S&P 500 index fund would beat hedge funds over 10 years, after fees.
lines.say: He bet that an S and P five hundred index fund would beat a group of hedge funds over ten years, after all fees.

lines.text: 2008 through 2017. Protégé Partners picked five funds of hedge funds.
lines.say: It ran from two thousand eight through twenty seventeen. A firm called Protégé Partners took the other side with five funds of hedge funds.

lines.text: Index fund: +125.8%. Hedge funds: +36.3% on average.
lines.say: The result: the index fund gained one hundred twenty-five point eight percent. The five hedge fund picks averaged thirty-six point three percent.

lines.text: The index won. The prize, about $2.2 million, went to Girls Inc. of Omaha.
lines.say: It wasn't close. The index won, and the prize, which had grown to about two point two million dollars, went to Girls Inc. of Omaha.

lines.text: $100 in the index fund became $225.80. At the funds' average: $136.30.
lines.say: In dollars, a hundred in the index fund became two hundred twenty-five dollars and eighty cents. At the hedge funds' average, one hundred thirty-six dollars and thirty cents.

lines.text: Buffett praised Jack Bogle in his 2016 letter.
lines.say: Buffett had already praised Bogle in his twenty sixteen shareholder letter.

lines.text: Buffett on Jack Bogle, in his 2016 letter.
lines.say: In his own words: if a statue is ever erected to honor the person who has done the most for American investors, the hands-down choice should be Jack Bogle.

scene.text: If a statue is ever erected to honor the person who has done the most for American investors, the hands-down choice should be Jack Bogle.

lines.text: Fair caveats: index funds never beat their index, and some active funds do win.
lines.say: Now, fair caveats. An index fund never beats its index; it matches it, minus a small fee. And some active funds do win, with odds that swing year to year.

lines.text: First half of 2026: 67% of large-cap funds trailed.
lines.say: In the first half of twenty twenty-six, the share that trailed fell to sixty-seven percent. Better for active, but still about two in three.

lines.text: Only about 25% of active funds survived and beat index rivals over 10 years.
lines.say: And Morningstar found that only about one in four active funds survived and beat their index-fund rivals over the ten years to June twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Chapter 4: The great takeover
lines.say: Chapter four: the great takeover.

lines.text: Passive share of US fund assets: 3% in 1995, 14% in 2005, 41% by March 2020.
lines.say: Now watch the money move. Passive held about three percent of US fund assets in nineteen ninety-five, fourteen percent in two thousand five, and forty-one percent by March twenty twenty.

lines.text: End of 2023: passive passed active, $13.25T to $13.24T.
lines.say: At the end of twenty twenty-three, passive passed active for the first time: about thirteen point two five trillion dollars to thirteen point two four trillion.

lines.text: End of 2025: over 55% (Morningstar).
lines.say: By the end of twenty twenty-five, passive held more than fifty-five percent, according to Morningstar.

lines.text: The US fund market flipped to passive.
lines.say: So in the US, the biggest pool of fund money now sits in funds that don't pick stocks at all.

lines.text: Why? Cheap, simple, and hard to beat.
lines.say: Why the takeover? Low cost, simple to understand, and a scoreboard that stock pickers rarely beat for long.

lines.text: BlackRock: a record $15.3T as of June 30, 2026.
lines.say: That flood made two firms enormous. BlackRock managed a record fifteen point three trillion dollars as of June thirtieth, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Vanguard: about $12T in 2026.
lines.say: Vanguard managed about twelve trillion dollars in twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: From $11.3M in 1976 to more than $1.6T in 2026.
lines.say: And Bogle's eleven point three million dollar folly? As the Vanguard five hundred Index Fund, it held more than one point six trillion dollars in twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: The folly became the default.
lines.say: The folly became the default.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Is passive too big?
lines.say: Chapter five: is passive too big?

lines.text: If a few firms own a slice of everything, does that change things?
lines.say: That raises a fair question: if a few firms own a slice of almost everything, does it change how companies behave?

lines.text: The Big Three: BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street.
lines.say: Most of that indexing runs through three firms, often called the Big Three: BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street.

lines.text: Their average combined stake in S&P 500 companies: 13.5% (2008) to 20.5% (2017).
lines.say: A twenty nineteen study by Lucian Bebchuk and Scott Hirst found their average combined stake in S and P five hundred companies rose from thirteen point five percent in two thousand eight to twenty point five percent in twenty seventeen.

lines.text: Together they cast about 25% of votes at S&P 500 meetings (2019 study).
lines.say: The same study found they cast about a quarter of all votes at S and P five hundred shareholder meetings.

lines.text: Common ownership: the same funds owning rival companies.
lines.say: Critics point to something called common ownership: the same funds owning big stakes in rival companies, like competing airlines.

lines.text: A 2018 study linked it to higher airfares. A 2022 study found no effect.
lines.say: A twenty eighteen study linked that overlap to higher airline ticket prices. A twenty twenty-two study of the same industry found no such effect. The debate continues.

lines.text: Index stock funds held about 18% of US stocks at the end of 2024 (ICI).
lines.say: Then again, index stock funds held only about eighteen percent of all US stock value at the end of twenty twenty-four, per the Investment Company Institute.

lines.text: Over half of fund assets, but under a fifth of the stock market.
lines.say: So index funds are over half of fund assets, yet they held under a fifth of the whole US stock market.

lines.text: One response: let fund investors vote.
lines.say: One response is pass-through voting, which lets some fund investors choose how their shares are voted.

lines.text: BlackRock offered Voting Choice on $3.96T of index stock assets (Dec 2025).
lines.say: As of December twenty twenty-five, BlackRock offered that choice on three point nine six trillion dollars of its index stock assets.

lines.text: Vanguard expanded its program in 2025: 12 funds, nearly 10 million investors.
lines.say: Vanguard expanded its own program in twenty twenty-five, to twelve funds and nearly ten million investors.

lines.text: Is passive too big? Still an open debate.
lines.say: So is passive too big? Researchers and regulators still disagree, and this video won't pick a side.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: 1. An index fund buys the whole scoreboard.
lines.say: One. An index fund doesn't pick. It buys the whole scoreboard, an idea Wall Street mocked as Bogle's Folly in nineteen seventy-six.

lines.text: 2. Fees compound: 0.05% vs 0.64% in 2025.
lines.say: Two. Fees compound. At the twenty twenty-five averages, zero point zero five percent versus zero point six four percent, the gap can reach thousands of dollars over thirty years.

lines.text: 3. Over 15 years, about 9 in 10 large-cap funds trailed.
lines.say: Three. Over the fifteen years to the end of twenty twenty-five, about nine in ten active large-cap funds trailed the S and P five hundred.

lines.text: 4. Passive passed active in 2023; over 55% by end-2025.
lines.say: Four. Passive passed active at the end of twenty twenty-three, and held more than fifty-five percent of US fund assets by the end of twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Open question: how big is too big?
lines.say: And one question is still open: what it means when a few giant firms hold a slice of almost everything.

lines.text: The boring idea held over 55% of US fund money by end-2025.
lines.say: So the boring idea that raised eleven point three million dollars held more than fifty-five percent of US fund money by the end of twenty twenty-five. Not bad for a folly.

lines.text: That's the money. Follow for more.
lines.say: That's the money. Follow for more.

post.title: Wall Street laughed at the first index mutual fund in 1976. By 2025, passive held 55%+
post.ig: In 1976, Wall Street called the first index mutual fund 'Bogle's Folly.' By the end of 2025, index-tracking funds held over 55% of US fund assets. Here's how the boring idea won.
post.tiktok: Wall Street laughed at this fund in 1976. Fifty years later, it holds more than $1.6 trillion.
post.yt_desc:
Index funds, explained from zero: why Wall Street mocked the first index mutual fund as "Bogle's Folly" in 1976 (it raised $11.3 million of a $150 million goal), and how index-tracking funds grew to more than 55% of US fund assets by the end of 2025. It covers Wells Fargo's 1971 pension index fund, the first US ETF (SPY, 1993), what fees really cost (0.05% vs 0.64% in 2025, and a hypothetical $10,000 over 30 years at an assumed 7%: $75,063 vs $63,584), the SPIVA long-term scorecards, and Warren Buffett's 2008-2017 bet against hedge funds. It ends with the debate over whether passive investing has grown too big: Big Three ownership stakes, common ownership research, and pass-through voting.

CHAPTERS

Sources: Vanguard and Morningstar (index fund 50th anniversary, August 2026); IFA, "Fifty Years of Bogle's Folly"; CFA Institute (July 2021) on the 1971 Wells Fargo fund; State Street (SPY); ICI, Trends in the Expenses and Fees of Funds, 2025 (March 2026) and earlier editions; ICI 2025 and 2026 Investment Company Fact Books; S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2025 (March 2026) and Mid-Year 2026 (September 2026); Morningstar US fund flows (January 2024, January 2026) and Active/Passive Barometer (mid-2026); Federal Reserve Bank of Boston working paper RPA 18-04; Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters (2016, 2017); CNBC (February 2017, February 2018, January 2024); BlackRock Q2 2026 results (July 2026) and 2026 Global Voting Spotlight; Vanguard (2026); Bebchuk and Hirst, "The Specter of the Giant Three" (2019); Azar, Schmalz and Tecu (Journal of Finance, 2018); Dennis, Gerardi and Schenone (Journal of Finance, 2022).

News and education, not financial advice.
